page_title: Building Blockchain in Go. Part 7: Network - Going the distance

summary.title: Building Blockchain in Go. Part 7: Network - Going the distance
summary.one_liner: You learn how a simplified blockchain network works in Go: nodes with roles (miner, full node, SPV), a version/inv/getdata/block/tx message protocol over TCP, and a multi-node scenario run on one machine using port-based node IDs.
takeaways: Blockchain nodes are both clients and servers; roles include miners, full nodes (validate blocks and transactions) and SPV nodes (verify a subset of transactions).
Messages are byte sequences with a 12-byte command name followed by a gob-encoded payload; version, getblocks, inv, getdata, block and tx form the core protocol.
Nodes are simulated on one machine by using ports as node IDs (localhost:3000, 3001, 3002) with separate database and wallet files per node.

A new node sends version to a hardcoded central node; if chain heights differ, blocks are requested via inv/getdata, and miners mine blocks from mempool transactions and broadcast inv for the new block.
The article is a simplified demo, not a real P2P network; it has known gaps such as no block validation and no check that requested data exists.
summary.summary: This final part of the series extends the Go blockchain into a networked system. It explains node roles (miner, full node, SPV), simplifies the setup by using localhost ports as node IDs, and describes the Bitcoin-like message types (version, getblocks, inv, getdata, block, tx) with Go code snippets for their handlers. It ends with a step-by-step command-line scenario where a central node, a wallet node and a miner node exchange transactions and blocks. The author notes the implementation is not a real P2P network and lists TODOs such as block validation and UTXO updates.
